554.title: Blessed is the one who spoke
554.hook: the opening blessing praises the one who spoke and the world came to be
554.howItsDone: Baruch She'amar opens the verses of song in the morning service; in many communities people stand for it, and those wearing a tallit hold the two front fringes and kiss them at the closing blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pesukei d'Zimra, the verses of song that warm the heart. Your line was warm up the heart. Today, the blessing that opens the songs.

Words make things happen. A judge says guilty, and a life changes. Two people say I do, and they're married. A friend says I'm sorry, and something heals. Most of the time, though, our words are cheap. We say we'll call and don't. We say five minutes and mean twenty. Now imagine a speaker whose every word becomes real, at once, with no gap. In many synagogues the room stands up for the blessing that praises exactly that.
screen: `WORDS MAKE THINGS HAPPEN.` → `MOSTLY, OUR WORDS ARE CHEAP.` → `A SPEAKER WITH NO GAP.`

segments.voice: It begins: baruch she'amar v'hayah ha'olam, blessed is the one who spoke, and the world came to be. It points back to the Torah's first page. In the old Jewish translation: "And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light." No tools, no raw materials in the story. Just speech, and then the world. Then the blessing builds, line after line, each starting with baruch, blessed. Blessed is the one who makes creation. Who says and does. Who decrees and fulfills. Who has mercy on the earth. Who has mercy on the creatures. Who rewards those who revere him. Who lives forever. Who redeems and rescues. Like a drumbeat. Notice two lines in the middle: mercy on the earth, and mercy on the creatures. The world isn't spoken into being and left; the same voice keeps caring for it. Customs gather around this blessing. Many people stand. Many who wear a prayer shawl hold its two front fringes during the blessing and kiss them at the end. A late tradition says the text came down from heaven on a written note, and that its words number eighty-seven. Whatever its history, it opens the songs with the most basic praise there is: the world exists because someone spoke, and kept their word.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SPOKE, AND THE WORLD WAS.` · `BARUCH, BARUCH, LIKE A DRUMBEAT.` · `MERCY ON THE EARTH AND CREATURES.` · `STAND, HOLD THE FRINGES, KISS.` · then, large: `BLESSED WHO SPOKE.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're about to start, a project, a meal, a conversation, a week, and put a pause before its first moment. If you pray, say baruch she'amar v'hayah ha'olam, blessed is the one who spoke and the world came to be; if not, notice that this new thing also begins with words. Then bring to mind one promise you've made lately, and decide to keep it.
Baruch She'amar. Blessed is the one who spoke: the blessing that opens the verses of song.
Your line: blessed who spoke. In this blessing, saying and doing are one and the same. See you tomorrow.

555.title: Give thanks (1 Chronicles 16:8)
555.hook: "O give thanks unto the LORD, call upon His name", David's song for the ark
555.carry: make known his doings among the peoples
555.howItsDone: Hodu, from 1 Chronicles 16, is said each morning in the verses of song: after Baruch She'amar in the Ashkenazi rite, and before it in many Sephardi rites.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baruch She'amar, blessed is the one who spoke. Your line was blessed who spoke. Today, the first song after that blessing.

The ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest that held the tablets, has been away for years: captured in battle, sent back, kept for months in one family's house. Now King David brings it up to Jerusalem. Music, shouting, the sound of horns. David himself dances. When the ark is set down in the tent he's pitched for it, there are offerings, and bread and cakes for everyone in the crowd. Then David does something meant to outlast the day. He puts singers in place, and hands them a song that begins with two Hebrew words: hodu ladonai.
screen: `THE ARK COMES HOME.` → `DAVID DANCES.` → `THEN HE APPOINTS SINGERS.`

segments.voice: The Book of Chronicles gives the song in full. In the old Jewish translation it opens: "O give thanks unto the LORD, call upon His name; make known His doings among the peoples." Near its end comes a line that runs all through Jewish prayer: "O give thanks unto the LORD; for He is good; for His mercy endureth for ever." The song is a weave. Its opening lines also appear in Psalm one hundred five, its middle in Psalm ninety-six, its close in Psalm one hundred six. Chronicles stitches them together for one great day. In the Ashkenazi prayer book, the passage comes right after Baruch She'amar; in many Sephardi prayer books, just before it. Either way, a morning of song begins where David began: with thanks. Notice the second half of that first verse: make known his doings among the peoples. Thanks here isn't only a private feeling. It's said out loud, so others hear the story. And hodu, give thanks, carries an echo. In Genesis, when Leah names her fourth son, she says: this time I will praise the LORD. His name is Judah, Yehudah, built from that same root. The tribe of Judah carries that name, and the word Jew comes from it too, through Yehudi. So a word for giving thanks sits close to the name the people carry.

segments.voice: Think of one person who did something good for you lately and didn't get much credit, a coworker who covered for you, a neighbor, a sibling, and shape one specific sentence of thanks you could say in front of others: not thanks for everything, but thanks for this. If you pray, you can say hodu ladonai, give thanks to the LORD.

556.title: Serve with gladness (Psalm 100)
556.hook: a thanksgiving psalm said on weekdays: "Serve the LORD with gladness"
556.carry: thanks is the part meant to last
556.howItsDone: In the Ashkenazi rite, Psalm 100 is said in the weekday verses of song, often while standing and with joy, and is left out on Shabbat, festivals, the eve of Passover, the intermediate days of Passover and the eve of Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hodu, David's song for the ark. Your line was make known his doings among the peoples. Today, a short psalm that's skipped on the holiest days.
screen: `MAKE KNOWN HIS DOINGS AMONG THE PEOPLES.`

segments.voice: There are two ways to wash the dishes. One with a sigh, scraping plates and counting the minutes. One with music on, maybe humming, warm water on your hands. Same dishes, same time, a completely different hour of your life. The difference isn't the task; it's the gladness you bring. Among the verses of song is a psalm only five verses long, and in its second verse it puts two words side by side, serve and gladness, as if they belong together.
screen: `TWO WAYS TO WASH THE DISHES.` → `SAME TASK, DIFFERENT HOUR.` → `SERVE, AND GLADNESS.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred has a heading, in the old Jewish translation: "A Psalm of thanksgiving." In Hebrew, mizmor l'todah. A todah was a particular Temple offering, the thanksgiving offering, brought by someone who'd come through danger: a journey, an illness, a prison. Then the psalm: "Shout unto the LORD, all the earth. Serve the LORD with gladness; come before His presence with singing." The Hebrew for serve, ivdu, shares its root with avodah, the word from the service of the heart, which means both work and worship. The same word for hauling stones and for prayer. The psalm says: do it with simchah, with joy. Now the surprise. In the Ashkenazi custom, this psalm is said on weekdays but skipped on Shabbat and festivals, because the thanksgiving offering, a personal, voluntary gift, wasn't brought on those days. It's skipped too before Passover and through the festival, because the thanksgiving offering included loaves of leavened bread. The prayer book remembers the Temple calendar even here. And a midrash says that in the time to come, all the offerings will cease except the thanksgiving offering, and all prayers will cease except the prayer of thanks. Some teachers say that's why this psalm should be said with real joy, even sung. Of everything in the service, thanks is the part meant to last.
screen: `MIZMOR L'TODAH: A PSALM OF THANKS.` · `AVODAH: WORK AND WORSHIP.` · `SKIPPED ON SHABBAT AND FESTIVALS.` · `ONLY THANKS WILL LAST.` · then, large: `SERVE WITH GLADNESS.`

segments.voice: Pick one chore waiting for you, dishes, email, laundry, the commute, and picture doing it the sighing way, noticing how it feels in your chest. Then picture it again, slower, with a song, with attention to the warm water or the sunlight through the bus window, and notice what changes. If you pray, you can say ivdu et Hashem b'simchah, serve the LORD with gladness.
Avodah, the Hebrew word for service, work and worship together, the root shared by Psalm one hundred's call to serve the Lord with gladness.

557.title: The missing letter (Berakhot 4b)
557.hook: Psalm 145 runs through the alphabet but skips nun, the teachers say to avoid a verse about falling
557.carry: the Lord upholdeth all that fall
557.howItsDone: Ashrei, built around Psalm 145, is said twice in the morning service and once in the afternoon service; in the morning it is the center of the verses of song.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm one hundred, the psalm of thanksgiving. Your line was thanks is the part meant to last. Today, a psalm said three times a day, and the letter it leaves out.
screen: `THANKS IS THE PART MEANT TO LAST.`

segments.voice: Psalm one hundred forty-five is an acrostic. Each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet: alef, bet, gimel, and on down the line. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, makes a large promise about it: whoever says it three times a day is assured a place in the world to come. It sits at the heart of the prayer called Ashrei. But count the verses. The Hebrew alphabet has twenty-two letters. This psalm has twenty-one verses. One letter, partway through, is missing.
screen: `AN ALPHABET PSALM.` → `SAID THREE TIMES A DAY.` → `ONE LETTER IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: The missing letter is nun, the letter for the sound N. The Talmud asks why. Rabbi Yochanan answers: because a terrible verse begins with nun. In the prophet Amos: fallen is the maiden Israel, she shall rise no more. Nafelah, fallen, starts with nun. So, the teachers say, the psalmist left the letter out rather than bring that word near a song of praise. Then another rabbi, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, adds the beautiful part. Even so, he says, David came back and caught them. Look at the very next verse, the one beginning with samech, the letter after nun. In the old Jewish translation: "The LORD upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that are bowed down." The word fall is right there, not as a sentence, but as something caught. The fall is acknowledged, then held. Now, what does the scholar hear? Among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a copy of this psalm that does have a nun verse: God is faithful in his words, and gracious in all his deeds. The ancient Greek translation has one too. So some scholars think a nun line once existed and dropped out of the traditional Hebrew text. The Talmud's reading doesn't depend on that question. It's a teaching about how to sing: you can leave a painful word unsaid, and still, in the next breath, say that the fallen are lifted.

segments.voice: Think back over the last few weeks for a moment when someone could have said the hard thing and didn't: a friend who let your mistake go, a parent who let a bad grade go, someone who changed the subject to spare you. Picture the word they didn't say, then what they did instead: a hand on your shoulder, a joke, a lift home. That's the samech after the missing nun.
Nun. The letter for the sound N, left out of Psalm one hundred forty-five, the Talmud says, so the song never speaks of falling without catching.
Your line: the Lord upholdeth all that fall. The hard word can stay unsaid, and the lifting still gets sung. See you tomorrow.

558.title: Five hallelujahs (Psalms 146–150)
558.hook: the last five psalms, each beginning and ending with praise
558.howItsDone: Psalms 146–150 are said every morning in the verses of song, right after Ashrei, with the last verse of Psalm 150 repeated; in many synagogues they are chanted quickly together, and the final verses are sung aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the missing letter in Psalm one hundred forty-five. Your line was the Lord upholdeth all that fall. Today, the five psalms that come right after it.

Hallelujah. It rings out in gospel choirs and in Handel's Messiah, turns up on greeting cards, and gets muttered when the bus finally comes. Said that way, it can sound like a sigh of relief. In Hebrew it's two words joined, and it's an instruction. In the Jewish morning service, right after Ashrei, it comes again and again, like bookends, at the start and end of each of the last five psalms in the Bible.
screen: `A WORD THAT TRAVELED.` → `IT'S HEBREW, AND AN INSTRUCTION.` → `BOOKENDS ON FIVE PSALMS.`

segments.voice: Hallelu means praise, said to a group: all of you, praise. Yah is a short form of God's name. So hallelujah is a call: everyone, praise God. Psalms one hundred forty-six through one hundred fifty each open and close with it: five psalms, ten hallelujahs. Listen to the praise widen. The first praises God for the people at the bottom: the prisoner, the blind, the stranger, the orphan, the widow. The second, in the old Jewish translation, says God is the one "Who healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds," and in the same breath counts the stars and calls each by name. The third calls on everything to praise: sun and moon, sea creatures, fire and hail, kings and children, old and young. The fourth asks for a new song. And the last is almost all music: horn, harp, drum, dancing, strings, pipes, cymbals, loud cymbals. Then the final line of the whole Book of Psalms: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Hallelujah." The prayer book says that line twice. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, records Rabbi Yose's wish to be among those who finish the praise every day, understood to mean these psalms. So the Book of Psalms, with all its grief and pleading, ends here: not with an answer, but with everything that breathes, praising.

Breathe in, notice your own breath, and think of three other things that breathe near you: a person, a pet, a tree outside. If you pray, end with hallelujah.
Five hallelujahs. Psalms one hundred forty-six to one hundred fifty, each opening and closing with hallelujah: all of you, praise God.
Your line: hallelujah. A call to everything that breathes, you included. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

559.title: The sea every morning (Exodus 15)
559.hook: the verses of song end with the Song of the Sea, sung daily
559.howItsDone: The Song of the Sea (Exodus 14:30–15:18) is said each morning near the end of the verses of song, often standing, and it is read from the Torah on the seventh day of Passover and on Shabbat Shirah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five hallelujahs that close the Book of Psalms. Your line was hallelujah. Today, the song those verses of song build toward.

A people who were slaves the week before stand on the far shore of a sea. Behind them, the water has closed. Ahead, the desert, and no idea what comes next. They crossed on dry ground, and they're exhausted, terrified and alive. And they sing. Moses sings, the people sing with him, and Miriam takes a drum while the women dance. Many scholars count it among the oldest poems in the Bible. Every morning, at the very end of the verses of song, Jews who pray the full service sing it again, as if they'd just stepped onto that shore.
screen: `SLAVES LAST WEEK.` → `ALIVE ON THE FAR SHORE.` → `THEY SING.`

segments.voice: It's called Shirat HaYam, the Song of the Sea, from Exodus fifteen. In the old Jewish translation it begins: "I will sing unto the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea." Then a line that turns up all over Jewish prayer: "The LORD is my strength and song." Even the way it's written is different. In a Torah scroll, this song isn't laid out in plain columns. The Talmud describes it as half bricks over whole bricks: short lines and gaps staggered like a wall, so you can spot it from across the room. The opening words are az yashir, then sang Moses. But the Hebrew verb can also be read as will sing, and the Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, hears a hint that the song isn't over, that it will be sung again in a world to come. Some commentators say to say it each morning with joy, as if you yourself had crossed that day. And there's a famous counterweight. The Talmud tells that when the Egyptians were drowning, the angels wanted to sing too, and God stopped them: the work of my hands is drowning in the sea, and you would sing? Israel's song of rescue is kept, every morning. But the tradition remembers that the rescue had a cost, and that God grieves for every creature.
screen: `SHIRAT HAYAM: THE SONG OF THE SEA.` · `WRITTEN LIKE A WALL OF BRICKS.` · `AZ YASHIR: SANG, OR WILL SING.` · `MY HANDIWORK IS DROWNING.` · then, large: `THE SEA SONG EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: Think of something you came through, an illness, a move, a loss, a terrible year, and picture yourself on its far shore. Then sing one line aloud, even softly, even off-key: ozi v'zimrat Yah, the LORD is my strength and song, if you know it, or a song you love if you don't. Let it go quiet, and remember someone who didn't make it through with you.
Shirat HaYam. The Song of the Sea, from Exodus fifteen, sung every morning at the end of the verses of song, as if just stepping onto that shore.
Your line: the sea song every day. The rescue is sung, and its cost remembered. See you tomorrow.

560.title: Yishtabach
560.hook: the closing blessing of the verses of song
560.howItsDone: Yishtabach closes the verses of song every morning, often said standing; it is followed by half Kaddish and the call to prayer, Barchu, which opens the Shema and its blessings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shirat HaYam, the Song of the Sea, sung every morning. Your line was the sea song every day. Today, the last word of the verses of song.

Every good piece of music knows how to end. The last chord of a symphony. The final chorus everyone sings. Even a playlist has a last song picked on purpose. Endings tell you what the whole thing was about. The verses of song have been building: the blessing for the one who spoke, David's thanks, the alphabet psalm, five hallelujahs, the sea. Then they close with a single paragraph. It adds no new idea. It gathers every word for praise it can find and stacks them, like a final chord.
screen: `ENDINGS SAY WHAT IT WAS ABOUT.` → `THE SONGS HAVE BEEN BUILDING.` → `A FINAL CHORD.`

segments.voice: It's called Yishtabach, from its first word: yishtabach shimcha la'ad malkeinu, may your name be praised forever, our king. Then the stack. To you belong song and praise, hallel and hymn, strength and dominion, victory, greatness and might, praise and glory, holiness and sovereignty, blessings and thanksgivings. Count them and you get fifteen. Commentators have connected that number to the fifteen Songs of Ascents in the Psalms, and to the fifteen steps in the Temple where, the Mishnah says, the Levites stood and sang. Notice the form. Most blessings start with baruch, blessed. Yishtabach doesn't, because it isn't a separate blessing. It's the closing half of Baruch She'amar, the blessing that opened the verses of song. The two are bookends around everything in between, and the custom is not to talk between them. Look at the opening words in Hebrew, too. The first letters of shimcha, la'ad, malkeinu and ha'el spell Shlomo, Solomon, and a tradition credits him with the prayer. That may be a later reading, but it shows how closely people have looked at every word. And the very last phrase calls God habocher b'shirei zimrah: the one who chooses songs of praise. Not the one who demands them. The one who chooses them, as if, out of everything in the world, the songs people sing are something God picks out and wants.
screen: `MAY YOUR NAME BE PRAISED FOREVER.` · `FIFTEEN WORDS OF PRAISE.` · `BOOKENDS WITH BARUCH SHE'AMAR.` · `THE ONE WHO CHOOSES SONGS.` · then, large: `PRAISED FOREVER.`

segments.voice: Think of the last thing you finished, a meal, a shift, this lesson, and before moving on, give it an ending. Stack the good things in it, the way Yishtabach stacks its words: it was warm, it was useful, someone laughed, it's done. If you pray, you can close with yishtabach shimcha la'ad, may your name be praised forever.
Yishtabach. May it be praised: the blessing that closes the verses of song with fifteen words of praise.
Your line: praised forever. A week of song ends here: the one who spoke, thanks, gladness, nun, five hallelujahs, the sea, and Yishtabach. Day five hundred sixty, done.
